summary: Specifies how Unicode can be used within MIME so email can carry text from many languages. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A way to put many alphabets into email so people everywhere can read them.

questions: how to send unicode in email
how is unicode encoded in mime
subtitle: How to label and send 16-bit Unicode text inside MIME mail, and how to name Unicode character sets.

tldr.problem: Internet mail supports only 7-bit US ASCII, and MIME did not list Unicode as a permitted character set or say how to encode it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers the character set name UNICODE-1-1, defines the text as two octets per character with the most significant octet first, and sets a naming pattern for future Unicode variants.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental memo. Mostly-ASCII text is meant to use the separate UTF-7 encoding from RFC 1642 instead.

today: RFC 1641 is an Experimental protocol memo and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is not an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Unicode Needs MIME
sections.content:
Unicode (Unicode 1.1, identical in repertoire and coding to ISO/IEC 10646-1:1993) is a 16-bit character set covering most of the world's writing systems. Internet mail as defined in RFC 822 supports only 7-bit US ASCII. MIME (RFC 1521 and RFC 1522) extends mail with other media types and character sets, but it neither lists Unicode nor says how to encode it, although it allows new character sets to be registered.

The authors see MIME as the most appropriate way to carry Unicode because it was designed for such extensions. A second goal is to let text that is mostly ASCII stay readable by mail clients that do not understand Unicode, which is covered by a separate document, UTF-7.
sections.eli5: Old email only knows a small alphabet. This memo teaches email how to carry letters from many languages.

sections.title: Choosing an Encoding
sections.content:
The memo gives guidelines and one specific usage: a straightforward use of Unicode as defined by the standard. It is meant for cases where sender and recipient do not want much processing, where the text is not mainly US-ASCII, or where both sides are known in advance to support Unicode.

For text that is mostly US-ASCII with occasional other characters, the memo points to UTF-7, which lets the ASCII part be read without Unicode support. Following RFC 1521, text that can be written in US-ASCII or ISO-8859-x should be, for maximum interoperability.
sections.eli5: Use the big alphabet only when you need it. If a message is almost all plain letters, a different method keeps it readable for everyone.

sections.title: The Unicode Character Set in Octets
sections.content:
The character set is serialized as octets, two per 16-bit character, with the most significant octet first. This matches ISO/IEC 10646-1:1993 for the UCS-2 form and the common network practice of one canonical transmission format. Text with an odd number of octets is ill-formed.

Because characters are 16 bits wide, the text would normally use the Binary or Base64 content transfer encodings. In header fields it would normally use the B encoding. The MIME character set identifier is UNICODE-1-1.
sections.eli5: Each letter is packed as two bytes, big end first, like writing a two-digit number tens digit first. A message with a stray extra byte is broken.

sections.title: Naming Unicode Variants
sections.content:
To let implementations check the Unicode version or ignore it, every registered MIME charset name for Unicode must follow one of two patterns: UNICODE-major-minor or UNICODE-major-minor-variant. The major and minor parts are decimal digits. The lowest version number compatible with the text should be used, and the lowest acceptable is UNICODE-1-1.

The optional variant names a transformation format, and with no variant the name means the basic two-octet form. The memo's hypothetical example is a UTF-8 form named UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8.
sections.eli5: Every version gets a tidy name tag, like Grade-1-1, so a reader can tell which edition of the alphabet book was used.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The memo shows two text/plain parts with charset=UNICODE-1-1 and Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64. The first carries the Japanese word for Japanese language, hexadecimal 65E5, 672C, 8A9E, encoded as ZeVnLIqe. The second carries the sequence 0041, 2262, 0391, 002E and is encoded as AEEiYgORAC4=.

The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: The memo shows real messages so you can see what a packed-up Japanese word looks like when it travels in mail.

data.title: Unicode text in a MIME part
data.code:
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UNICODE-1-1
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64

ZeVnLIqe
